title: Philippines Deploys Diwata-1, Its First Filipino-Built Microsatellite
reason: Confirmed by JAXA's official press release and multiple university sources: Diwata-1, the Philippines' first microsatellite, launched to the ISS in March 2016 aboard Cygnus CRS-6 and was deployed from the Kibo module on 27 April 2016 (JAXA's first success of a 50kg-class microsatellite deployment). It was built by Filipino engineers (the 'Magnificent 9' team) from the University of the Philippines Diliman and DOST-ASTI, in partnership with Japan's Tohoku University and Hokkaido University. It carried three earth-observation instruments (High Precision Telescope, Space-borne Multispectral Imager, Wide Field Camera) and its mission ended in early 2020 (decommissioned/re-entered atmosphere around April 2020), matching 'operated until 2020.' All material facts in the description are corroborated by independent, authoritative sources (JAXA, Hokkaido University, Tohoku University, DOST-ASTI).

verifications.reason: Confirmed via JAXA's official press release and multiple university/agency sources: Diwata-1 was carried to the ISS in March 2016 and deployed from the Kibo module on 27 April 2016 — JAXA's release is titled "Successful Deployment of DIWATA-1, First Microsatellite developed by the Republic of the Philippines, from ISS Kibo." It was built by a team of Filipino engineers (the "Magnificent 9") from DOST-ASTI and University of the Philippines Diliman, in partnership with Japan's Tohoku University (bus development) and Hokkaido University, per eoPortal, Tohoku University, and Hokkaido University sources. It carried three Earth-observation instruments (High Precision Telescope, Space-borne Multispectral Imager, Wide Field Camera) per eoPortal/CEOS. Per Inquirer and the PHL-Microsat project blog, Diwata-1 was decommissioned and re-entered the atmosphere around April 2020, matching "operated until 2020." All material details (country, year, actors, instrument count, end date) check out.

title: Growth of OFW Precursor Labor Migration
reason: The broad trend described is well-documented: Filipino labor migration abroad grew steadily through the 1950s as a precursor to the later mass OFW phenomenon, involving both US-linked professional migration and Pacific/Asia construction contract labor. Guampedia's dedicated history "Filipino Migration to Guam 1945-1975" documents that following a 1947 US-Philippine labor recruitment agreement, Filipino workers filled the bulk of the Guam construction workforce (up to 65% by 1950), and "by the mid-1950s, BPM [Brown-Pacific-Maxon] employed more than 17,000 laborers" on US-territory Pacific construction projects — directly overlapping the 1956 timeframe and matching the description's "construction projects in Asia and the Pacific." Multiple secondary sources (Wikipedia's Overseas Filipino Worker article, IIAS "Laboring pioneers" piece, Philippine DOLE historical accounts) independently corroborate that non-professional contract labor migration to Asia (Sabah/Sarawak logging, Pacific construction) and continued postwar professional emigration to the US mainland were both underway and expanding across the 1950s-1960s, explicitly framed by historians as the pre-1974 "Filipino Pioneers" era that laid groundwork for the formal OFW program. No source pins a single discrete 1956 event, but this is a multi-year growth trend, and 1956 falls squarely within the documented expansion window; nothing found contradicts the description or suggests it belongs to a different, non-adjacent year. The remittance detail is a plausible, consistent inference (wages of 30-50 cents/hour on Guam already exceeded homeland pay) though not separately verified in isolation for 1956.

verifications.reason: Multiple independent sources corroborate this as an accurate characterization of Philippine labor emigration trends in the mid-1950s, of which 1956 was squarely a part. (1) Guampedia's history of Filipino migration to Guam confirms that by the mid-1950s the U.S. Navy's Base Facilities/Base Property Maintenance program employed 'more than 17,000 laborers' from the Philippines in construction camp-cities (e.g., Camp Roxas, 7,000 workers), with the downturn only beginning in the 'late 1950s' amid an economic slump — i.e., 1956 falls within the active growth/peak period, not the decline. (2) Independent aggregated search results (DOLE historical accounts, IIAS, Center for Migrant Advocacy) confirm the Philippine government formally recognized and began managing this outward migration in 1956 itself, establishing the Manila Employment Office with a mandate to encourage 'domestic as well as overseas migration' and creating a parallel Overseas and Fee-charging Employment Agencies Unit — a direct institutional precursor to the later POEA/OFW system. (3) Migration to the United States specifically also grew in this era via the 1948 Exchange Visitor Program, under which Filipino nurses (and other professionals) began arriving in large numbers through the 1950s-60s (over 11,000 nurses by the 1960s), consistent with the description's emphasis on U.S.-bound migration alongside Pacific/Asia construction work (Guam, Wake Island, and Sabah/Sarawak logging camps). Combined, the country, year, and substance (growing overseas labor migration to the US and Asia-Pacific construction, laying groundwork for the later OFW phenomenon, with remittances a natural corollary) are all corroborated. This is a broad multi-year sociological trend rather than a single dated event, but 1956 is well within — not adjacent to — the documented active-growth window, so no year correction is warranted.
